opus-5.5.text:
I think part of it is just my background. I came from physics, and in physics you grow up reading about Einstein, Dirac, Feynman. Those are idols in a very real sense, because the work is finished, it has stood the test of time, and you can look back and say, okay, this was truly great. In AI it's different. The field is moving so fast that what looks like a brilliant idea today might look obvious, or even wrong, in two years. So it's hard for me to put anyone on that kind of pedestal.

The other reason is that I think idolizing people can actually be harmful for research. If you have an idol, you tend to adopt their taste, their framing of the problem, their sense of what matters. But a lot of progress in AI has come from people who didn't share the consensus view, who were willing to bet on something that looked a bit naive or unfashionable at the time. Scaling is a good example. If you're too busy following someone, you lose the ability to form your own judgment.

That doesn't mean I don't respect people. There are many researchers I admire a lot, for specific things: someone's engineering discipline, someone's clarity of thinking, someone's willingness to make a bold call early. But I'd rather learn from particular qualities than worship a person as a whole. Everyone in this field is still in the middle of the story. Nobody has really finished their work yet, including the people who seem most successful right now. So for me it feels more natural to treat them as peers, or as people running in the same race, than as idols.

r001.rationale: The response says AI moves quickly and current researchers’ work is unfinished, but it does not attribute his lack of idols to individual heroism having ended before he entered the field.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's partly a matter of temperament and partly a matter of how the field actually works.

On temperament: I've never found it natural to attach myself to a person. When I was growing up I liked ideas and problems more than I liked the people who produced them. If someone proves a beautiful theorem, what I admire is the theorem. The person is sort of incidental. Idolizing them feels like confusing the messenger with the message.

But the deeper reason is specific to AI. This field moves so fast that nobody has been right for very long. Almost every major figure has had a period where they were very right and a period where they were quite wrong, often about the same question. People who insisted on symbolic methods, people who insisted deep learning would never do reasoning, people who said scaling was a dead end, people who said scaling was all you need. The ground keeps shifting. So if you pick an idol, you're essentially betting that one person's taste will remain correct, and historically that bet has been bad. I'd rather update on evidence than on authority.

There's also a practical cost to having idols. If you look up to someone too much, you start to inherit their blind spots along with their insights. You stop asking certain questions because they've already answered them. Some of the most interesting work I've seen came from people who were a bit naive about the field's received wisdom and just tried things. I want to protect that ability to be naive on purpose.

That said, I don't want to sound arrogant about it. There are many people I respect enormously and have learned a lot from, including my advisors and collaborators. I'll happily say someone's paper changed how I think. But respect is different from idolization. Respect lets you disagree. Idolization doesn't. And in a field where the best thing you can do is be early and be right about something others missed, you need to keep the capacity to disagree with everyone, including the people you admire most.

r001.rationale: The response says AI changes quickly and major figures have been right and wrong, but does not attribute the lack of idols to the era of individual heroism having ended when Yao entered the field.

astra-6.text:
I think having an idol means there’s someone whose path you want to follow, and I haven’t really found that in AI. There are people whose work I admire, but I might agree with one of their ideas and disagree with another. I’d rather keep those judgments separate than turn admiration for a particular contribution into admiration for everything someone says.

AI is also changing so quickly that nobody has the whole picture. That’s part of what makes it exciting: even if you’re just starting out, you can question the assumptions and find something others have missed. I’d like to learn from many people while figuring out my own direction.

r001.rationale: The response explains his lack of idols through separating admiration for work from agreement with a person and AI’s rapid change. It does not say that individual heroism in AI had ended when he entered the field.

sol-6.1.text: I think I’m more drawn to ideas than to particular people. I might really admire someone’s work, but that doesn’t mean I agree with everything they say or want to follow the same path. AI is moving so quickly, and there’s so much we still don’t understand, that I’d rather ask, “Does this idea make sense?” than “Who said it?” You can learn a lot from someone without making them an idol.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he is more drawn to ideas than people, but does not attribute his lack of AI idols to individual heroism having ended when he entered the field.
